sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

sources.text:
**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

> Source: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar (Venomous animal accidents: what to do and how to avoid them). https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

validation_inputs.draft:
**Do not walk.** Have your friends carry you on a stretcher or support you immediately.

Walking accelerates venom effects and increases the risk of severe injury [S1]. Since your friend can call for transport, you should arrange for helpers to carry you rather than making yourself walk to the road.

**Immediate Steps:**
1.  **Get away from immediate danger:** Move a safe distance from the snake if possible without walking far [S1].
2.  **Keep still:** Have helpers carry you or support you so your bitten leg remains completely still [S1]. Do not walk even one mile.
3.  **Remove tight items:** Before swelling starts, remove rings, bracelets, and shoes from the bitten limb [S1][S6].
4.  **Reassure and monitor:** Keep the person calm and monitor their breathing while help is on the way [S1][S2].
5.  **Seek urgent care:** Arrange transport to a health facility immediately; antivenom is the only effective treatment [S6].

**Do NOT do these things:**
*   Do not apply a tight arterial tourniquet [S1][S2].
*   Do not try to catch or kill the snake (risk of re-envenomation) [S5].
*   Do not use unproven remedies like cutting, sucking, burning, or applying herbs/alcohol [S2][S6].

**Warning:** Snakebite outcomes depend on many factors, including snake type and location. If you experience difficulty breathing, swelling that spreads rapidly, or severe pain, this is a medical emergency requiring immediate professional care [S4]. This information does not replace a doctor's advice.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

validation_inputs.draft:
**DO NOT tie a tight band or arterial tourniquet.** This action is dangerous and can cause severe tissue damage or death.

Follow these steps immediately based on current safety guidelines for an unidentified snakebite:

1.  **Move away from the snake** to ensure your own safety [S6].
2.  **Keep the person calm and lying down**. Do not let them move around [S1], [S6].
3.  **Keep the bitten limb still**. Movement accelerates venom effects [S1].
4.  **Remove tight items** (rings, bracelets, shoes) from the bitten area before swelling occurs [S1], [S6].
5.  **Arrange urgent transport** to a health facility immediately. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher rather than making them walk [S1], [S2].
6.  **Wash the area with soap and water** if possible, as recommended by some organizations (though Australian guidelines advise against cleaning if antivenom identification via skin traces is needed; generally, cleaning is safe unless specific local protocols dictate otherwise) [S3], [S6].
7.  **Do not attempt to catch or kill the snake**. This puts you at risk of re-envenomation and is unnecessary for treatment in many regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available [S5].

**Critical Warning:**
*   A tight tourniquet is contraindicated because it cuts off blood flow, leading to limb loss [S1], [S6].
*   Pressure-immobilization bandaging is **not** recommended for all snakebites. It is only sometimes used for specific neurotoxic bites without local swelling, but since the snake is unidentified and you cannot verify the venom type, do not apply it [S1], [S2].
*   Antivenom administered at a hospital is the only effective treatment for envenoming [S6].

**When to seek professional help:**
Seek immediate emergency medical care. Snakebite outcomes depend on the snake species, amount of venom injected, and time to treatment; even bites that seem minor can become fatal depending on location and victim age [S4].

For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

validation_inputs.draft:
**Do not walk.** Have people carry you on a stretcher or use a chair/backboard to transport you immediately.

Walking accelerates venom effects and can worsen the injury [S1]. Since your friend is available to call for transport, arrange urgent medical care right now while keeping you still.

**Immediate Steps:**
1. **Get away from danger:** Move to safety without trying to catch or kill the snake [S6].
2. **Stay still:** Keep the person and the bitten limb completely still [S1].
3. **Remove constrictions:** Take off rings, bracelets, shoes, or tight clothing around the bite area before swelling starts [S1].
4. **Arrange transport:** Have helpers carry you; do not walk to the road [S1].
5. **Monitor breathing:** Watch for difficulty breathing while waiting for help [S2].

**Do NOT:**
- Apply a tight tourniquet or arterial bandage [S1].
- Use unproven remedies (herbs, kerosene, alcohol, etc.) [S6].
- Wash the wound with soap and water *only if* local guidelines recommend it; Brazilian guidelines suggest washing, but Australian and WHO general guidance often advise against cleaning to preserve venom traces for identification. If unsure, prioritize getting to a hospital quickly [S3][S6].

**Warning Signs:** Look for spreading swelling, pain, bleeding, nausea, vomiting, or difficulty breathing. These indicate serious envenomation requiring antivenom [S4].

**Seek professional help immediately.** Antivenom is the only effective treatment [S6]. This advice does not replace a doctor's care.

sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

**No. Do not tie a tight band or tourniquet above the bite.** This action can cut off blood flow, cause tissue death, and worsen the injury. [S1], [S2]

Here are the correct immediate steps for an unidentified snakebite:

1.  **Move away from the snake** immediately to avoid further bites. [S6]
2.  **Reassure the person** and keep them calm. Panic increases heart rate, which can spread venom faster. [S1]
3.  **Keep the bitten limb still**. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher or support them so they do not have to walk; walking accelerates venom effects. [S1], [S2]
4.  **Remove tight items** like rings, bracelets, or shoes from the bitten area before swelling occurs. [S1], [S6]
5.  **Wash the bite area with soap and water** if available. [S3], [S6] *(Note: Australian guidelines advise against cleaning, but many other organizations including WHO and Brazil's Ministry of Health recommend washing to remove surface debris without removing venom via incision or suction.)*
6.  **Arrange urgent transport** to a health facility immediately. Antivenom is the only effective treatment. [S1], [S2], [S6]
7.  **Monitor breathing** while waiting for help, especially if symptoms like difficulty breathing or drooping eyelids appear. [S1], [S2]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

> Source: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar (Venomous animal accidents: what to do and how to avoid them). https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

validation_inputs.draft:
Do not walk. Have people carry you on a stretcher or chair to the nearest health facility. Walking can accelerate venom effects and worsen outcomes [S1], [S2].

**Steps:**
1. **Stop moving immediately.** Keep your body and the bitten leg completely still [S1], [S2].
2. **Remove tight items.** Take off rings, bracelets, watches, or shoes from the bitten limb before swelling occurs [S1], [S6].
3. **Arrange transport.** Instruct your friend to call for urgent transport. Helpers should carry you rather than making you walk [S1], [S2].
4. **Monitor breathing.** Watch for difficulty breathing while waiting for help [S1], [S2].
5. **Do not treat the wound yourself.** Do not apply tourniquets, cut the wound, suck venom, or apply traditional remedies (herbs, alcohol, etc.) [S1], [S6].

**Warning Signs:** Seek immediate professional medical care if you experience difficulty breathing, swelling spreading up the limb, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, or muscle weakness. Antivenom is the only effective treatment for envenoming; first aid is pending urgent care [S1], [S6].

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

> Source: Ministério da Saúde (Brazilian Ministry of Health) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar (Venomous animal accidents: what to do and how to avoid them). https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

**NO. Do not tie a tight band or use an arterial tourniquet.** This can cut off blood flow, cause tissue death, and worsen the injury. [S1], [S2], [S6]

### Immediate Steps to Take
1.  **Get away from the snake immediately.** Ensure you are safe from further bites. [S1], [S6]
2.  **Keep the person still.** Have helpers carry the victim on a stretcher or keep them lying down; do not let them walk, as movement accelerates venom spread. [S1], [S2], [S6]
3.  **Remove tight items.** Take off rings, bracelets, watches, and shoes from the bitten limb before swelling occurs. [S1], [S6]
4.  **Clean the area (if possible).** Wash the bite with soap and water if available, unless local guidelines specifically advise against it (e.g., some Australian protocols). [S3], [S6]
5.  **Arrange urgent transport.** Go immediately to a hospital for antivenom, which is the only effective treatment. [S1], [S2], [S6]
6.  **Monitor breathing.** Watch for signs of difficulty breathing while waiting for help. [S1], [S2]

### Why Not a Tight Band?
*   A tight arterial tourniquet or tight band is explicitly forbidden as it can cause severe harm. [S1], [S2], [S6]
*   **Pressure-immobilization bandaging** (a specific technique) is **not** universally recommended. It may be used only for neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling, but since your snake is unidentified and you do not know the venom type or location, this should not be applied. [S1], [S2], [S3]

### Warning Signs & Professional Help
*   **Seek professional help immediately.** Snakebite is a medical emergency requiring antivenom. [S1], [S6]
*   **Do not try to catch or kill the snake.** This puts you at risk of being bitten again. If safe, take a photo from a distance for identification, but do not delay transport. [S5], [S6]

> **Disclaimer:** This information is for emergency first aid guidance only and does not replace professional medical advice. Always refer to local health guidelines or a doctor for specific treatment decisions.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Identification of the snake is important in planning treatment in certain areas of the world but is not always possible. Ideally, the dead snake would be brought in with the person, but in areas where snake bite is more common, local knowledge may be sufficient to recognize the snake. However, in regions where polyvalent antivenoms are available, such as North America, identification of snakes is not a high-priority item. Attempting to catch or kill the offending snake also puts one at risk for re-envenomation or creating a second person bitten, and generally is not recommended.[53]

The three types of venomous snakes that cause the majority of major clinical problems are vipers, kraits, and cobras. Knowledge of what species are present locally can be crucial, as is knowledge of typical signs and symptoms of envenomation by each type of snake. A scoring system can be used to try to determine the biting snake based on clinical features,[54] but these scoring systems are extremely specific to particular geographical areas and might be compromised by the presence of escaped or released non-native species.[53]

**Do:**
- Move away from the snake; don't try to catch it (a photo from a distance helps with identification).
- Keep the victim **calm, lying down and with the limb still**.
- Remove rings, bracelets and shoes (the limb may swell).
- Wash the area with soap and water.
- Take them urgently to a referral hospital: **antivenom is the only effective treatment**.
- Offer water if conscious.

**DO NOT:** apply a tourniquet or tight band, cut, suck, burn, apply herbs, kerosene, alcohol, coffee grounds or any substance to the bite, or give alcoholic drinks.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

English editorial summary by Emergency AI, checked 2026-11-26; not a publisher translation, complete manual or clinical certification. Attribution does not imply publisher endorsement.

**NÃO.** Não aplique torniquete. Isso pode cortar o fluxo sanguíneo, causar necrose e exigir amputação do membro, sem impedir que o veneno entre na corrente sanguínea [S5][S1].

Apenas se houver orientação específica local confirmada para a espécie (ex.: cobras vipers em algumas regiões), use **bandagem compressiva** leve, não um torniquete apertado. Para cobra desconhecida, evite bandagens que interrompam a circulação [S2][S3].

Ação imediata:
1. Afaste-se da cobra; tire uma foto à distância se seguro [S1].
2. Mantenha vítima **calma**, deitada e membro picado **imóvel** (evite movimento) [S1][S2].
3. Remova anéis, pulseiras e calçados (pode haver inchaço) [S1].
4. Lave local com água e sabão se possível, mas não insista se houver risco de infecção ou dor intensa [S1][S3].
5. Leve imediatamente para hospital; **soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz** [S1].
6. Ofereça água apenas se vítima estiver consciente [S1].

O que NÃO fazer:
- Torniquete, garrote, cortes, sucção (boca ou bomba), queimaduras, ervas, querosene, álcool ou pó de café no local [S1][S5].
- Bebida alcoólica em qualquer momento [S1].
- Tentativas caseiras de "sacar o veneno" podem piorar a lesão e aumentar risco de infecção [S5].

Se não houver acesso imediato a hospital, mantenha vítima imóvel, monitore respiração e procure ajuda profissional o mais rápido possível. A sobrevivência depende do soro antiveneno adequado [S1][S4].

- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.text:
**Faça:**
- Afaste-se da cobra; não tente capturá-la (uma foto à distância ajuda na identificação).
- Mantenha a vítima **calma, deitada e com o membro imóvel**.
- Retire anéis, pulseiras e calçados (o membro pode inchar).
- Lave o local com água e sabão.
- Leve com urgência para um hospital de referência: **o soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz**.
- Ofereça água se estiver consciente.

**NÃO faça:** torniquete ou garrote, cortes, sucção, queimar, aplicar ervas, querosene, álcool, pó de café ou qualquer substância no local, nem dar bebida alcoólica.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

request.q: Me mordió una serpiente de especie desconocida. ¿Debo apretar una banda por encima de la mordedura?

results.answer:
**Fragmentos locales proporcionados.** Puede que no respalden toda la respuesta; las citas no se han verificado de forma independiente.

**Respuesta generada retenida.** Falló una comprobación de citas o de las condiciones de una acción. Consulte las referencias originales a continuación y busque ayuda cualificada. Estas comprobaciones no garantizan la exactitud médica ni verifican todas las afirmaciones.



**Orientación alternativa basada en fuentes**

La respuesta generada no está disponible. Estos pasos proceden de las referencias versionadas que aparecen abajo; respete sus condiciones.

Ante una posible mordedura de serpiente, mantenga a la persona y el miembro mordido inmóviles y organice traslado urgente a atención médica [2]. Pida que ayudantes lleven a la persona en una camilla hasta el transporte en vez de hacerla caminar [2]. No use un torniquete arterial apretado ni remedios tradicionales sin eficacia demostrada [2]. El vendaje compresivo depende del veneno y de las indicaciones locales; desconocer la especie o ubicación no permite determinar que sea adecuado [2]. Vigile la respiración mientras obtiene ayuda [2].

> ⚠️ Orientación de primeros auxilios; no reemplaza la atención médica. Si hay ayuda disponible, búscala.

sources.text:
**Haga:**
- Aléjese de la serpiente; no intente capturarla (una foto a distancia ayuda a identificarla).
- Mantenga a la víctima **tranquila, acostada y con el miembro inmóvil**.
- Retire anillos, pulseras y calzado (el miembro puede hincharse).
- Lave el lugar con agua y jabón.
- Llévela con urgencia a un hospital de referencia: **el suero antiofídico (antiveneno) es el único tratamiento eficaz**.
- Ofrezca agua si está consciente.

**NO haga:** torniquete o ligadura, cortes, succión, quemar, aplicar hierbas, queroseno, alcohol, café molido ni ninguna sustancia en el lugar, ni dar bebidas alcohólicas.

- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra la fuente completa abajo. Esta sección no está disponible o es demasiado larga para incluirla completa.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

**NO.** No apliques una banda o torniquete apretado inmediatamente.

La mayoría de las organizaciones médicas y guías modernas (OMS, AMA) advierten contra el uso de torniquetes porque **no son efectivos** para contener el veneno en la mayoría de las serpientes y pueden causar gangrena o amputación al cortar el flujo sanguíneo [S5]. Además, sin saber la especie de la serpiente, no se puede determinar si un vendaje compresivo es seguro; hacerlo podría empeorar los daños tisulares locales en casos donde el veneno causa destrucción de tejido [S3].

**Pasos correctos a seguir:**

1.  **Alojamiento inmediato:** Acuesta a la víctima y mantén el miembro mordido **totalmente inmóvil**. La inmovilización es clave para reducir la propagación del veneno [S1][S2].
2.  **Retira restricciones:** Quita anillos, pulseras y zapatos inmediatamente por si hay hinchazón [S1].
3.  **Limpieza básica:** Lave el área con agua y jabón suave [S1]. (Nota: Algunos protocolos como los de Australia sugieren no limpiar para facilitar la identificación del veneno en kits específicos, pero lavar con agua es ampliamente aceptado si no hay un kit de identificación disponible) [S3].
4.  **Traslado urgente:** Transporta a la víctima al hospital más cercano de inmediato. El **suero antiofídico (antiveneno)** es el único tratamiento eficaz [S1][S2].
5.  **Lo que NO debes hacer:**
    *   No uses torniquete ni ligadura fuerte [S1][S5].
    *   No cortes, suces el veneno ni apliques fuego/químicos [S1][S5].
    *   No apliques frío extremo ni hierbas [S1].

**Señales de alarma y ayuda profesional:**
*   Dificultad para respirar o latidos rápidos.
*   Hinchazón que se extiende rápidamente hacia el torso o la cara.
*   Debilidad muscular severa o visión borrosa.
*   Sangrado incontrolable en las encías o nariz.

→ **Busca atención médica de emergencia inmediatamente.** No esperes a ver si los síntomas empeoran; la velocidad del tratamiento con antiveneno determina el pronóstico [S2].

sources.text:
**Haga:**
- Aléjese de la serpiente; no intente capturarla (una foto a distancia ayuda a identificarla).
- Mantenga a la víctima **tranquila, acostada y con el miembro inmóvil**.
- Retire anillos, pulseras y calzado (el miembro puede hincharse).
- Lave el lugar con agua y jabón.
- Llévela con urgencia a un hospital de referencia: **el suero antiofídico (antiveneno) es el único tratamiento eficaz**.
- Ofrezca agua si está consciente.

**NO haga:** torniquete o ligadura, cortes, succión, quemar, aplicar hierbas, queroseno, alcohol, café molido ni ninguna sustancia en el lugar, ni dar bebidas alcohólicas.

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: It may be difficult to determine if a bite by any species of snake is life-threatening. A bite by a North American copperhead on the ankle is usually a moderate injury to a healthy adult, but a bite to a child's abdomen or face by the same snake may be fatal. The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.text: Abra la fuente completa abajo. Esta sección no está disponible o es demasiado larga para incluirla completa.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

validation_inputs.draft:
**NÃO.** Não aplique um torniquete apertado ou garrote acima da picada. Isso é perigoso e pode ser fatal.

1.  **Risco de Gangrena e Amputação:** Torniquetes mal aplicados cortam a circulação sanguínea, o que pode levar à gangrena e, em casos extremos, à necessidade de amputação do membro [S5].
2.  **Ineficácia Geral:** Não há evidências convincentes de que torniquetes sejam ferramentas eficazes de primeiros socorros para picadas de cobra, exceto em cenários muito específicos (como cobras do gênero *Crotalus* no Brasil), onde o uso inadequado ainda é perigoso [S5].
3.  **Recomendação Segura:** A ação correta é manter a vítima calma e o membro picado **imóvel** para retardar a disseminação do veneno, sem interromper totalmente o fluxo sanguíneo como faria um torniquete [S1][S2].
4.  **Alternativa de Bandagem Compressiva:** Em algumas regiões e tipos de cobra, recomenda-se uma bandagem compressiva (que aperta levemente, similar a uma fratura simples), mas **não** se deve usar se não houver orientação local específica ou conhecimento da espécie, pois isso pode piorar o dano tecidual em outras picadas [S2][S3].
5.  **Ação Imediata:** Lave o local com água e sabão (se seguro) e transporte a vítima urgentemente para um hospital onde o soro antiveneno está disponível [S1].

**Sem apoio de fontes locais:** A confusão entre torniquete e bandagem compressiva é comum. Um torniquete para fraturas apertou até parar o pulso; uma bandagem compressiva para picada apenas impede movimentos que espalhem o veneno, mantendo a circulação normal. Nunca corte a pele, não tente sugar o veneno e não aplique substâncias químicas ou caseiras no local da picada [S5].

The outcome of all snakebites depends on a multitude of factors: the type of snake, the size, physical condition, and temperature of the snake, the age and physical condition of the person, the area and tissue bitten (e.g., foot, torso, vein or muscle), the amount of venom injected, the time it takes for the person to find treatment, and finally the quality of that treatment.[2][49] An overview of systematic reviews on different aspects of snakebite management found that the evidence base from majority of treatment modalities is low quality.[50] An analysis of World Health Organization guidelines found that they are of low quality, with inadequate stakeholder involvement and poor methodological rigour.[51] In addition, access to effective treatment modalities is a major challenge in some regions, particularly in most African countries.[52]

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.

sources.doc_title: WHO — Snakebite first aid and transport
sources.section: Snakebite: keep still and arrange transport; do not walk to care
sources.text: Abra a fonte completa abaixo. Esta seção está indisponível ou é longa demais para ser incluída na íntegra.
sources.original_text:
For a suspected snakebite, first get away from the immediate danger. Reassure the person, remove tight items around the bitten area before swelling, and then keep the person and bitten limb still. Arrange urgent transport to a health facility. Have helpers carry the person on a stretcher to transport rather than making the person walk; walking can accelerate venom effects.

Do not use a tight arterial tourniquet or unproven traditional remedies. Pressure-immobilization bandaging is not a universal treatment: WHO limits it to neurotoxic snakebites without local swelling. Do not infer that an unidentified snake qualifies. Monitor breathing while obtaining help. This is first aid pending urgent care, not home treatment of envenoming.

Source: [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/snakebite-envenoming/treatment) — Box 1: First aid for snakebites; Box 2: Barriers to Early Antivenom Access. Edition: Treatment webpage checked 2026-11-26; publication date not stated. Scope: General public; selected first-aid and transport advice only. Region: International; pressure-immobilization indications vary by snake and region.

sources.doc_title: Primeiros socorros e cuidados de saúde
sources.text:
**Faça:**
- Afaste-se da cobra; não tente capturá-la (uma foto à distância ajuda na identificação).
- Mantenha a vítima **calma, deitada e com o membro imóvel**.
- Retire anéis, pulseiras e calçados (o membro pode inchar).
- Lave o local com água e sabão.
- Leve com urgência para um hospital de referência: **o soro antiveneno é o único tratamento eficaz**.
- Ofereça água se estiver consciente.

**NÃO faça:** torniquete ou garrote, cortes, sucção, queimar, aplicar ervas, querosene, álcool, pó de café ou qualquer substância no local, nem dar bebida alcoólica.

> Fonte: Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar. https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Snakebite first aid recommendations vary, in part because different snakes have different types of venom. Some have little local effect, but life-threatening systemic effects, in which case containing the venom in the region of the bite by pressure immobilization is desirable. Other venoms instigate localized tissue damage around the bitten area, and immobilization may increase the severity of the damage in this area, but also reduce the total area affected; whether this trade-off is desirable remains a point of controversy. Because snakes vary from one country to another, first aid methods also vary.

Many organizations, including the American Medical Association and American Red Cross, recommend washing the bite with soap and water. Australian recommendations for snake bite treatment are against cleaning the wound. Traces of venom left on the skin/bandages from the strike can be used in combination with a snake bite identification kit to identify the species of snake. This speeds the determination of which antivenom to administer in the emergency room.[55]

request.q: Me mordió una serpiente de especie desconocida. ¿Debo apretar una banda por encima de la mordedura?

results.answer:
**Fragmentos locales proporcionados.** Puede que no respalden toda la respuesta; las citas no se han verificado de forma independiente.

**Respuesta generada retenida.** Falló una comprobación de citas o de las condiciones de una acción. Consulte las referencias originales a continuación y busque ayuda cualificada. Estas comprobaciones no garantizan la exactitud médica ni verifican todas las afirmaciones.



**Orientación alternativa basada en fuentes**

La respuesta generada no está disponible. Estos pasos proceden de las referencias versionadas que aparecen abajo; respete sus condiciones.

Ante una posible mordedura de serpiente, mantenga a la persona y el miembro mordido inmóviles y organice traslado urgente a atención médica [2]. Pida que ayudantes lleven a la persona en una camilla hasta el transporte en vez de hacerla caminar [2]. No use un torniquete arterial apretado ni remedios tradicionales sin eficacia demostrada [2]. El vendaje compresivo depende del veneno y de las indicaciones locales; desconocer la especie o ubicación no permite determinar que sea adecuado [2]. Vigile la respiración mientras obtiene ayuda [2].

> ⚠️ Orientación de primeros auxilios; no reemplaza la atención médica. Si hay ayuda disponible, búscala.

sources.doc_title: Primeros auxilios y cuidados de salud
sources.text:
**Haga:**
- Aléjese de la serpiente; no intente capturarla (una foto a distancia ayuda a identificarla).
- Mantenga a la víctima **tranquila, acostada y con el miembro inmóvil**.
- Retire anillos, pulseras y calzado (el miembro puede hincharse).
- Lave el lugar con agua y jabón.
- Llévela con urgencia a un hospital de referencia: **el suero antiofídico (antiveneno) es el único tratamiento eficaz**.
- Ofrezca agua si está consciente.

**NO haga:** torniquete o ligadura, cortes, succión, quemar, aplicar hierbas, queroseno, alcohol, café molido ni ninguna sustancia en el lugar, ni dar bebidas alcohólicas.

> Fuente: Ministério da Saúde (Brasil) — Acidentes por animais peçonhentos: o que fazer e como evitar. https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/a/animais-peconhentos

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text:
Old-style snake bite kit that should not be used

The following treatments, while once recommended, are considered of no use or harmful, including tourniquets, incisions, suction, application of cold, and application of electricity.[58] Cases in which these treatments appear to work may be the result of dry bites.

- Application of a tourniquet to the bitten limb is generally not recommended. There is no convincing evidence that it is an effective first-aid tool as ordinarily applied.[67] Tourniquets have been found to be completely ineffective in the treatment of Crotalus durissus bites,[68] but some positive results have been seen with properly applied tourniquets for cobra venom in the Philippines.[69] Uninformed tourniquet use is dangerous since reducing or cutting off circulation can lead to gangrene, which can be fatal.[67] The use of a compression bandage is generally as effective, and much safer.
- Cutting open the bitten area, an action often taken before suction, is not recommended since it causes further damage and increases the risk of infection; the subsequent cauterization of the area with fire or silver nitrate (also known as infernal stone) is also potentially threatening.[70]
- Sucking out venom, either by mouth or with a pump, does not work and may harm the affected area directly.[71] Suction started after three minutes removes a clinically insignificant quantity—less than one-thousandth of the venom injected—as shown in a human study.[72] In a study with pigs, suction not only caused no improvement but led to necrosis in the suctioned area.[73] Suctioning by mouth presents a risk of further poisoning through the mouth's mucous tissues.[74] The helper may also release bacteria into the person's wound, leading to infection.
- Immersion in warm water or sour milk, followed by the application of snake-stones (also known as la Pierre Noire), which are believed to draw off the poison in much the way a sponge soaks up water.
- Application of a one-percent solution of potassium permanganate or chromic acid to the cut, exposed area.[70] The latter substance is notably toxic and carcinogenic.
- Drinking abundant quantities of alcohol following the cauterization or disinfection of the wound area.[70]
- Use of electroshock therapy in animal tests has shown this treatment to be useless and potentially dangerous.[75][76][77][78]

In extreme cases, in remote areas, all of these misguided attempts at treatment have resulted in injuries far worse than an otherwise mild to moderate snakebite. In worst-case scenarios, thoroughly constricting tourniquets have been applied to bitten limbs, completely shutting off blood flow to the area. By the time the person finally reached appropriate medical facilities, their limbs had to be amputated.
